summary: Of the 636 people who were regular attenders a year ago, 94 (14.8%) have gone completely quiet, with no check-in for themselves or their kids, no group, serving, form or event registration. That is at the top of the 10–15% healthy range, and another 112 (17.6%) are still around but no longer regular. We are replacing them, but only about one for one: 88 to 137 newcomers became regular and are still here, against 94 who lapsed. Underneath the Sunday numbers we are essentially flat. The losses concentrate among young adults, singles and people in their first year, and they cluster from April to June. Stepping back from serving is the clearest early warning.

answers.attrition: 14.8% annual attrition (94 of 636), at the top of the 10–15% healthy range. That counts every kind of activity in Planning Center except giving: check-ins (including a child checked in by their household), groups, serving, forms and event registrations. Counted by household it is 11.6% (39 of 337), inside the range, because many losses are one family member drifting rather than whole families leaving.
answers.breakouts: Young adults (18–29: 28%), the CYA ministry (32%), single adults (24%) and people in their first year (26%) lapse at roughly twice the rate of people with 3+ years at the church (11%) and adults 65+ (10%). Being in a group or on a team did not change the outright lapse rate much (14% vs 16%), but it did keep people regular: 76% of those in a group and serving are still regular, against 61% of those in neither.
answers.funnel: Half of first-time guests never come back. Of guests who have had four months to settle in, 50% returned, 39% came a third time, 19% became regular and 10% connected to a group or team. The two biggest leaks are between the first and second visit, and between the third visit and becoming regular.
answers.net_growth: Essentially flat. Between 88 and 137 newcomers became regular and are still active, against 94 lapsed regulars, so the net is −6 to +43 depending on how strictly a first-time guest is defined. The count of regular attenders rose from 636 to 721, but most of that rise comes from adults being checked in more consistently since February. Among under-18s, whose check-in recording was steady, regulars fell from 239 to 225.
answers.seasonality: Losses cluster from April to June: 88 of the 149 measurable losses (59%) were people whose last visit fell in those three months, the stretch after Easter into summer. First-time guests peaked in August and September 2026 (104 and 126). This is one year of data, so treat it as a pattern to watch, not a settled trend.
answers.early_warning: Three to six months before their last visit, lapsed people were 2.8 times as likely to have stopped serving, and about 1.6 to 1.7 times as likely to have halved their attendance or dropped out of their group, compared with people who stayed. In the final three months the gaps widen: 4.5 times for stopping serving and 2.7 times for attendance halving. They were also lighter attenders from the start: 9.7 attendance days in the baseline quarter, against 10.9 for those who stayed.

findings: Attrition is at the top of the healthy range. 14.8% of last year's regular attenders (94 of 636) have had no activity of any kind in 90 days: no check-in for themselves or their kids, no group, serving, form or event registration. Counted by household it is 11.6% (39 of 337). Only 68% of last year's regulars are still regular today.

We lose young adults, singles and newcomers first. 28% of regular attenders aged 18–29 lapsed (17 of 61), and 32% of those whose main ministry was CYA (12 of 38). Single adults lapsed at 24% (15 of 63) and first-year people at 26% (22 of 86). People with 3+ years at the church lapsed at 11% and adults 65+ at 10%.

The front door works; the second step doesn't. 742 first-time guests came in the last 12 months. Half never returned, and of those with four months to settle in only 19% became regular and 10% connected to a group or team.

We are flat underneath the Sunday numbers. Newcomers who stuck (88–137) roughly match regulars who left (94). Sunday adult check-ins doubled from February 2026, but kids' and volunteers' check-ins held steady, so most of that rise is better recording, not growth.

Stopping serving is the clearest warning, and spring is when people slip away. People who stopped serving were 2.8 times as likely to lapse in the following three to six months, and 59% of losses came after visits in April–June.

recommendations.title: Assimilation and follow-up: win the second visit.
recommendations.body: Set up a Planning Center Workflow that creates a card automatically for every first-time guest. A named person calls or texts within 48 hours with a specific invitation for next Sunday, and personally invites them to Discover Celebration by their third visit. Review the workflow weekly in staff meeting. The target is to move the return rate from 50% to 60% and the regular rate from 19% to 25% over the next year.

recommendations.title: Serving: make Dream Team leaders the early-warning system.
recommendations.body: When a regular volunteer has not served or has declined for six weeks, their team leader (not staff) reaches out within a week. Once a month, walk through the private at-risk list (73 people today) by ministry, with an owner and an outcome noted for each name. Help every first-year attender find a team by their third month, since serving is what most clearly holds people.

recommendations.title: Groups: build a young-adult on-ramp, take attendance, and plan for spring.
recommendations.body: Invite every CY Night and 18–29 regular into a short-term group within a month. Require every group to record attendance in Planning Center: 38% of group meetings had none, and 39 of 206 groups never recorded any, which hides who is drifting. Because most losses start after Easter, launch a spring group semester and a serving push in the weeks right after Easter, rather than letting the calendar go quiet into summer.

gaps.title: Giving is not included.
gaps.body: The Planning Center connector account isn't authorized to read Giving, so lapsed means no check-in (for themselves or a child in their household), group attendance, confirmed serving, form submission or event registration. Some of the 94 lapsed people may still be giving, so attrition is somewhat overstated, and the giving breakout could not be built. Ask the Planning Center Organization Administrator to give the connector account Giving access, then re-run.

gaps.title: Adult check-in coverage changed mid-year.
gaps.body: Sunday Experience averaged about 105–170 people checked in per Sunday before February 2026 and 220–360 after, while kids and volunteers held steady. Adults who attend without being checked in are invisible, so the baseline cohort leans toward kids, volunteers and group members, and recent adult growth is overstated. The household rate (11.9%) and the under-18 comparison are the most reliable views.

gaps.title: Some Sunday check-ins are entered late.
gaps.body: Some Sunday Experience records were entered up to two weeks after the service, so the most recent Sundays may be incomplete. A few people on the at-risk list may simply have recent visits not yet entered.

gaps.title: Group attendance is incomplete.
gaps.body: 38% of the 1,555 group meetings since July 2025 have no attendance recorded, and 39 of 206 groups never recorded any. Group engagement is therefore undercounted, and the group-dropout warning sign is weaker than it would be with complete records.

gaps.title: History starts July 2025.
gaps.body: Data was pulled through the Planning Center connector, one page at a time, from July 14, 2025 on (about 105,000 activity records across Check-Ins, Groups, Services, People forms and Registrations, each batch checked against Planning Center's own count, with spot-checks of individual records). Tenure therefore comes from the date each People record was created. A first-time guest is counted only if their People record was created within 60 days of the first visit, which can miss guests with an older record (for example from a past event). The −6 to +43 range on net growth reflects this. Check-in history back to January 2023 was pulled separately for the year-by-year comparison.

gaps.title: No service-time or campus split.
gaps.body: Check-ins are recorded against one session per Sunday, not a specific service time, so attrition by service time is not measurable. There is one campus.

gaps.title: The database is much larger than the active church.
gaps.body: Planning Center lists 9,541 active people, but only 4,105 had any activity in the last 15 months (a check-in for themselves or their kids, group, serving, form or event registration). Planning Center's active status is not a usable measure of attendance. There are also 32 possible duplicate person records, and 25 household records with 9 or more members, which are treated as a separate category.

gaps.title: Some segments are small.
gaps.body: Students (34 regulars), CYA (38) and single adults (63) are small groups, so read their rates as directional. One-time-guest check-ins with no person record (80 in the last year) cannot be followed at all.

gaps.title: Staff notes are shown, not counted.
gaps.body: The 6,086 notes on People profiles are written by staff, so they are not counted as the person's own activity: a note like "called, no answer" would otherwise hide someone who has left. The private follow-up lists show each person's most recent note date instead, so you can see who has already been contacted. Note text was not pulled.

gaps.title: Forms and registrations: what counts.
gaps.body: Form submissions count as activity, except 2,254 submissions on internal staff forms (purchase orders, check requests, time sheets, reimbursements, graphic and facilities requests). 158 of the first-time guests had an earlier form, registration or child check-in before their own first check-in, usually because adults weren't routinely checked in before February 2026, so some guests' first visit was earlier than the check-in data shows.
